lines: Thunder shook the square hard enough to rattle every loose shutter.
Lightning split the old fence by the fields. I helped pull the burning boards away.
The bell rang during the storm, but the thunder swallowed half the warning.
I went door to door after the worst strike and made sure everyone answered.
Rain found three leaks in the meeting house and one directly over my head.
The golem stood in the square through all of it. I stayed somewhere drier.
We brought the animals in before the lightning reached the pasture.
Every candle went out at once, so we sat together until someone found flint.
A tree came down across the north path. We cleared enough room to reach the homes beyond it.
Nobody was left outside when the sky turned white. That is what matters.
I held a shutter closed until my arms went numb.
One strike cracked the well cover. It needs replacing before anyone leans on it.
The paths became mud before the storm was halfway done.
The children counted the seconds after each flash. The adults pretended not to.
I have never heard the village go so quiet between thunderclaps.
We filled every spare bucket from the roof runoff. At least the rain made itself useful.
Several doors swelled shut in the wet. I helped pry them open this morning.
My hands stopped shaking before the windows did.
Today we check roofs, mend shutters, and move the fallen branches.
I still have no trade, but holding a lantern for the roof crews is work enough today.
Smoke reached the square before anyone could see which roof was burning.
We passed buckets hand to hand until my arms forgot how to lower themselves.
I helped move the children and elders away from the wind.
The fire jumped one fence before we soaked the next one.
Someone kept ringing the bell while the rest of us shouted directions over it.
We saved the houses first and worried about the sheds afterward.
I carried water, wet blankets, and one very angry cat.
The heat drove us back from the first doorway. We found another way inside.
A neighbor came through the smoke coughing, but walking. I nearly sat down from relief.
The well path stayed clear because everyone dropped what they were doing to help.
Sparks landed on the dry roofs across the lane. We watched them until dawn.
The fire is out, but the village still smells like wet ash.
I found three missing people by asking who had last seen them, not by guessing.
One wall is gone. Everyone who slept behind it is safe.
We tore down a burning awning before it could carry the flames farther.
My sleeves are singed, and I was nowhere near the bravest person there.
The animals panicked at the smoke, so we opened the far pen and led them around.
Today we clear the blackened timber and make sure nothing is still hot underneath.
Nobody asked about my profession when the bucket line needed another pair of hands.
We lost things in that fire. We did not lose each other.
The first horn sent everyone in the square running for a door.
I helped bar the meeting house while the defenders took the lane outside.
Crossbow bolts struck the walls close enough to shake dust into our hair.
We counted people after every wave because nobody trusted the quiet.
I carried food and bandages to the defenders between attacks.
The golem held the gate longer than any of us expected.
One family could not reach their home, so we made room for them in ours.
The bell rope burned my hands, but I kept ringing until the last neighbor was inside.
Raiders tried the narrow lane and found half the village waiting for them.
I saw farm tools used like weapons and weapons used with more restraint than I expected.
The children stayed under the floor until the horns stopped.
We moved the wounded through back doors so the main path stayed clear.
A bolt broke the window beside me. I am still finding glass in the room.
The final wave felt longer because we knew how tired everyone was.
Nobody cheered right away. We listened first and made sure it was truly over.
I spent the morning returning dropped supplies to whoever still needed them.
The gate needs repair, but it held when people were behind it.
I was afraid the whole time. I helped anyway.
Before the next horn, every latch and shelter path needs checking.
The village survived because everyone found one useful thing to do and kept doing it.
The first warning came from someone shouting beyond the torchlight.
I woke to pounding on a door that was not mine.
We lit every lantern we could find and closed the dark gaps between houses.
I guided two children across the square while the defenders watched the lane.
Something moved behind the pens, so we brought the animals closer to the homes.
The shadows looked dangerous long after the attackers were gone.
One loose latch nearly cost us a safe room. It has been replaced.
I carried spare torches until there were none left in the chest.
Nobody slept after the first cry. We waited together for daylight.
The golem kept turning toward sounds the rest of us could not hear.
We found tracks between the houses when the sun came up.
A broken lantern left the east path dark at the worst moment.
I stayed near the well and called out whenever someone crossed the square.
The doors shook hard enough to wake everyone inside.
We used the meeting house because its walls were stronger than our nerves.
Dawn made the damage look smaller and the exhaustion look worse.
I checked every home after sunrise and did not leave until someone answered.
Tonight we need more torches, stronger latches, and fewer empty watch posts.
I still turn when I hear footsteps outside after dark.
Surviving the night was not brave work. It was neighbors refusing to leave one another alone.
The wind threw sand through every crack in the village.
We tied cloth over our faces before crossing the square.
The main path vanished so quickly that neighbors used ropes between doors.
I helped move the animals into the nearest solid shelter.
Sand packed the hinges until several doors would not open.
The sky turned brown at midday, and every torch looked weak beneath it.
We could hear people coughing in the next house but could not see the doorway.
I spent the storm clearing one vent so the room could breathe.
The well cover kept most of the grit out. The bucket was another story.
A loose roof tile crossed the square faster than anyone should.
We marked the shelter doors with lanterns so nobody walked past them.
The children stayed low while the adults tried to sound less worried than they were.
Sand buried the lower fence and left the gate hanging crooked.
I found grit in my boots, my bed, and a sealed bread jar.
No one went missing, though we counted twice to be certain.
The wind stopped suddenly. The whole village kept listening anyway.
Today we free the doors, clear the paths, and check every roof fastening.
The animals are safe, but they will not go near the east pen yet.
I carried water to anyone still coughing after the air cleared.
A spare pair of hands is useful when half the village needs digging out.
Snow piled against the doors faster than we could clear it.
We kept the meeting house warm for anyone whose hearth went cold.
I carried firewood indoors until I could no longer feel my fingers.
The path to the well disappeared before morning.
Neighbors dug toward one another from both ends of the lane.
We followed the bell by sound when the square vanished in the snow.
One set of footprints stopped near the fence. We found the villager sheltering in the shed.
The animals crowded together, so we brought extra hay and closed every gap.
Cold found the weak wall in three homes. We moved those families before dark.
I kept a pot warm while others cleared the roofs.
The wind pushed snow under the door no matter how many cloths we packed around it.
We tied a rope from the meeting house to the nearest homes.
A roof beam started groaning under the weight, so everyone got out before it cracked.
The woodpile emptied faster than anyone planned.
Morning came bright enough to hurt our eyes and cold enough to freeze the hinges.
I checked on the quiet houses first. Silence feels different in a storm.
Today we open the paths, clear the roofs, and refill every wood stack.
My boots are still wet, but every neighbor made it through the night.
The bell rope froze stiff. We had to pull it together.
I do not need a trade to know when someone needs warmth and a shovel.
